title: The Voice-First AI Overlay: Designing Conversational Co-Pilots - Gregory Bruss
talk_summary: This is a design/UX talk about voice-first AI overlays that assist live human-to-human conversations without becoming a third speaker. It covers design principles (transparency, low cognitive load, progressive autonomy) and engineering challenges (debouncing, context repair, timing, attention cost), but offers no concrete orchestration, cost, or review techniques.

takeaways.what_they_do: When listening to a live stream, they debounce partial inputs so the agent doesn't fire on every pause or breath, only on meaningful boundaries.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when someone is speaking, they might pause to take a breath... debouncing is quite important there

takeaways.what_they_do: They explicitly treat 'context repair' as a first-class pipeline stage so suggestions match what is currently happening, not stale state.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Context repair is also very important. If you aim to give live assistance, then you're probably working with a sub-second speed limit.

takeaways.what_they_do: They treat attention as currency: every hint taxes the user, so hints must be timely, relevant, dismissible, and never spam.
takeaways.evidence_quote: attention is a kind of currency and every time uh a hint arrives it taxes the attention of the person that's seeing it

takeaways.what_they_do: They let users moderate how much assistance they get over time, ramping help down as competence grows.
takeaways.evidence_quote: allowing progressive autonomy. So in some cases, you know, if you're new to a field or something, you need a lot of help at the beginning

takeaways.what_they_do: They flag speculative execution and caching as a promising direction for reducing latency in the overlay pipeline.
takeaways.evidence_quote: speculative execution and and caching that's also quite interesting
